meta.label: Federated social servers
tradeoffLabels: most transparent about who runs it
meta.attribution: Built from software licence files, project documentation, sign-up and pricing pages, instances' own published site data, and operators' own pages about who runs and funds them, read directly, plus one European Commission enforcement decision, not from review sites. Openness reflects the software licence and whether the service is built on an open protocol (ActivityPub) rather than a closed one; Bluesky is included because its AT Protocol is open and supports federated hosting, but it does not speak ActivityPub, and its openness score says so; accessibility covers both the hardware a server needs and how easily a person can sign up to use one that already exists. Transparency reflects whether a reader can find out who actually runs and funds a server. A server's software being open source does not make the people running a given instance trustworthy; only what that operator publishes about itself does. Suggest changes via Contribute.

reads.text: Compare federated social servers by disclosure, everyday access, openness, and support life.

axes.label: Access or disclosure
axes.question: Easier joining or clearer operator disclosure?

products.name: Mastodon (software)
products.description: The most widely run ActivityPub server software, self-hosted on a server you control or joined on someone else's instance.

openness.note: The repository's licence badge and LICENSE file mark Mastodon under the GNU Affero General Public License v3, and the README describes it as a 'free, open-source social network server' built on the ActivityPub standard, interoperating with other servers as a federated network.

accessibility.note: The repository lists Ruby 3.3 or newer, PostgreSQL 14+, Redis 7.0+, Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg 5.1+ as prerequisites, and documents Docker, docker-compose, Heroku and Scalingo deployment options alongside a standalone install, a heavier stack than several other options here.

longevity.note: Mastodon's own docs describe an account-migration feature that moves your followers to a new server, but warn that 'your posts will not be moved, due to technical limitations,' media cannot be imported automatically, and there is a 30-day cooldown before you can migrate again.

products.name: GoToSocial
products.description: A lightweight, Golang-based ActivityPub server built to run on very little hardware, compatible with Mastodon-style apps.

openness.note: GoToSocial is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3; the README explains that anyone running a modified version over a network must offer users the corresponding source.

accessibility.note: The README says GoToSocial 'uses only about 250-350MiB of RAM, and requires very little CPU power, so it plays nice with single-board computers, old laptops and tiny $5/month VPSes,' and describes it as an ActivityPub server built to let people connect 'without tracking or targeted advertising.'

products.name: Pleroma
products.description: A microblogging ActivityPub server built in Elixir, designed to run comfortably on modest hardware.

openness.note: Pleroma's project page states the software is licensed AGPL-3, with documentation and other content separately under CC-BY-4.0 and CC-BY-SA-4.0, and describes it as 'a microblogging server software that can federate...with other servers that support ActivityPub.'

accessibility.note: The project page says Pleroma 'can run on low-power devices like Raspberry Pi... but can scale well when ran on more powerful hardware,' built on Elixir with PostgreSQL for storage.

products.name: Akkoma
products.description: An ActivityPub server compatible with both Mastodon and Pleroma-style clients, run as its own project rather than as a patch to another one.

openness.note: Akkoma's documentation states it is 'free software licensed under the AGPLv3,' and describes it as 'a federated social networking platform, compatible with Mastodon and other ActivityPub implementations,' shipping both its own frontend and the Mastodon frontend as an alternative interface.

products.name: Misskey
products.description: An ActivityPub-compatible microblogging server with its own distinct interface and feature set, originating in Japan.

openness.note: The repository's licence badge marks Misskey AGPL-3.0, and the README describes it as 'a completely free and open interplanetary-microblogging platform' and 'an open source, federated social media platform.'

products.name: Pixelfed
products.description: A photo-sharing ActivityPub server built as a federated alternative to Instagram, without an algorithmic feed.

openness.note: The README states Pixelfed is 'open-sourced software licensed under the AGPL license,' describing itself as letting photos 'find their audience naturally, without algorithmic barriers' while joining the wider fediverse.

products.name: PeerTube
products.description: A federated, partly peer-to-peer video platform built as an alternative to YouTube, maintained by the French nonprofit Framasoft.

openness.note: The repository's licence is AGPL-3.0, and the README describes PeerTube as 'a free, decentralized and federated video platform developed as an alternative to other platforms that centralize our data and attention, such as YouTube, Dailymotion or Vimeo,' developed by Framasoft.

accessibility.note: PeerTube's FAQ gives concrete minimums: 1 vCore and 1.5 GB of RAM plus a 20Mbit/s upload link for a small instance, scaling to 4 vCore, 4 GB of RAM and 1Gbit/s upload for around 1,000 concurrent viewers, and 8 vCore/8 GB if video transcoding runs on the same machine.

products.name: Friendica
products.description: An ActivityPub and Diaspora-compatible server built to link a single account across several federated networks at once.

openness.note: The repository's licence is AGPL-3.0, and the README describes Friendica as 'a platform for decentralised social communication linking to other independent social and corporate services,' interacting with Mastodon, Lemmy, Diaspora and others across the fediverse.

products.name: mastodon.social
products.description: The flagship Mastodon server, run by the company behind the software rather than self-hosted, the default door into the fediverse for most new users.

accessibility.note: Mastodon's own homepage offers 'Join mastodon.social' as its primary call to action, ahead of an option to 'pick another server'; separate signup documentation describes three possible registration modes, open, invite-based, or requiring moderator approval, without stating which one mastodon.social itself currently uses.

transparency.note: Mastodon's about page says mastodon.social is run by Mastodon GmbH, a German company subject to the EU Digital Services Act, after the project's earlier non-profit gGmbH status was lost when Germany removed software projects from eligibility; a separately incorporated US 501(c)(3), Mastodon Inc., now supports the project's growth and accepts tax-deductible donations.

products.name: Fosstodon
products.description: A Mastodon instance for people interested in free and open source software, run by a community foundation rather than a company.

transparency.note: Fosstodon's foundation announcement says it is organised as 'a legally recognized nonprofit' with a three-member board, formed so the community 'remains independent and aligned with its original mission' instead of being subject to corporate ownership, and funded by 'donations, grants, and other funding mechanisms.'

longevity.note: The same announcement says the foundation's board will prepare annual financial statements for transparency, and that if the foundation were ever to dissolve, its funds would be distributed to other open-source projects rather than to any individual.

products.name: masto.host
products.description: Paid managed hosting that runs a stock Mastodon server for you, the route where someone else administers the software but you keep the ability to leave.

economical.note: Masto.host's pricing page lists tiers from $6 a month (Moon) up to $89 a month (Galaxy) plus a custom option, and states 'custom Mastodon forks, other Activity Pub software and code changes are not supported,' meaning it only ever runs stock Mastodon.

longevity.note: The same page says 'you can migrate in and out of Masto.host whenever you like,' with linked guides for both directions, and that configuration, media and database storage 'are backed up daily to a remote secure object storage.'

transparency.note: The pricing page describes plans and support in detail but does not name who operates the service, stating only that 'this website and service is not affiliated with or endorsed by Mastodon GmbH or Mastodon Inc.'

products.name: X (Twitter)
products.description: The mainstream centralized platform most people already use, included as the honest floor this whole family of decisions is an alternative to.

accessibility.note: X's App Store listing shows it is free to download with in-app purchases for X Premium, describing the app around breaking news, trending topics and Grok, an AI assistant it says is 'powered by X's live data.'

transparency.note: The European Commission fined X 120 million euros under the Digital Services Act, citing a 'Blue checkmark' verified-account design it found deceptive and an advertising repository that does not meet the DSA's transparency requirements.

openness.note: The same Commission decision names X's 'failure to provide researchers access to public data' as one of the three violations behind the fine, unlike the ActivityPub-based options in this roster, whose protocol and data are open by design.

products.name: Threads (Meta)
products.description: Meta's mainstream text app, centralized by default but with an opt-in feature that shares public posts into the fediverse over ActivityPub.

accessibility.note: Threads' App Store listing shows it is free to download, ranked number 1 in the Social Networking category with 2.2 million ratings, built around starting and replying to threads, trending topics and direct messages.

openness.note: Meta's engineering blog says Threads users aged 18 or over with public profiles 'can now choose to federate their profiles' over ActivityPub so posts appear on other fediverse servers, but the feature is opt-in, does not yet show fediverse likes or replies back on Threads, and excludes posts with restricted replies or polls.

products.name: Lemmy
products.description: A Reddit-style link aggregator and forum server written in Rust, whose communities federate with each other and with the wider fediverse.

openness.note: Lemmy's README lists it as open source under the AGPL licence and explains that 'anyone can easily run a server, and all these servers are federated (think email)', joined to the wider fediverse.

accessibility.note: Lemmy's user documentation says that because it is written in Rust it 'has very low hardware requirements' and 'can easily run on a Raspberry Pi or similar low-powered hardware.'

longevity.note: The same page says users can download a backup of their account from the settings page and import it on another Lemmy instance. The backup covers display name, bio, settings, followed communities, saved posts and blocks. The page does not list a user's own posts or comments, and imported follows and blocks are added to the new account rather than moved.

transparency.note: The README names where the money comes from: Lemmy is 'free, open-source software, meaning no advertising, monetizing, or venture capital, ever', paid for by user donations and a grant from the NLnet foundation. It does not publish accounts.

products.name: lemmy.world
products.description: A large general-purpose Lemmy instance run by a Dutch volunteer foundation that also operates mastodon.world, a no-install way into fediverse forums.

transparency.note: The Fedihosting Foundation's about page says it is 'a non-profit foundation based in the Netherlands', founded by two fediverse admins in December 2023, and that it runs about 20 instances including Lemmy.World. The footer gives its Dutch Chamber of Commerce (KvK) number, and the navigation links to donation pages. No financial statements are linked from the page.

accessibility.note: lemmy.world's public site data shows registration set to require an application, so a new account waits for moderator approval. The instance reports about 200,000 registered users and about 12,600 active in the past month. Its sidebar warns that you cannot post or comment while connected through a VPN or Tor.

products.name: Mbin
products.description: A community-run fork and continuation of /kbin: a link aggregator, forum and microblogging server on ActivityPub, written in PHP.

openness.note: Mbin's README marks it AGPL-3.0 and describes 'a decentralized content aggregator, voting, discussion, and microblogging platform running on the fediverse' that talks to Mastodon, Lemmy, Pixelfed, Pleroma and PeerTube over ActivityPub. It calls itself 'a fork and continuation of' /kbin, run by community consensus.

accessibility.note: The README's requirements list PHP 8.5 or newer, Node 24 or newer, a web server (NGINX, Apache or Caddy), PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ and Valkey, KeyDB or Redis, with Mercure optional. That is one of the heavier stacks in this roster.

products.name: Sharkey
products.description: A Misskey-derived ActivityPub microblogging server that adds the Mastodon client API and sign-up approval for moderators.

openness.note: Sharkey's README describes an 'open source, decentralized social media platform' whose ActivityPub support lets users follow people on Mastodon and Pixelfed. The repository's LICENSE file is the GNU Affero General Public License v3.

accessibility.note: Sharkey's install guide lists 'more than 2GB of free RAM, we recommend at least 4GB', Node.js 22.11 or later, PostgreSQL 15 or later, Redis, FFmpeg and a C build toolchain, with a Docker Compose route as the alternative. That is similar to Mastodon's footprint.

products.name: Iceshrimp.NET
products.description: A ground-up .NET rewrite of the Iceshrimp ActivityPub server, still labelled beta, with no flagship instance and commercialisation listed as an anti-goal.

openness.note: The README describes Iceshrimp as 'a decentralized and federated social networking service, implementing the ActivityPub standard' and tests its Mastodon-compatible API against common clients. The repository's LICENSE file is the European Union Public Licence 1.2, a copyleft licence. The README also says this is still beta software.

products.name: WriteFreely
products.description: A minimalist blogging server written in Go, whose blogs can be followed from Mastodon and other ActivityPub software; the team also sells hosted instances through Write.as.

openness.note: WriteFreely's README says it is licensed under the AGPL, copyright Musing Studio LLC and contributors. It says WriteFreely sites can connect with communities running WriteFreely, Plume or 'other ActivityPub-powered software'.

accessibility.note: WriteFreely's homepage says it is written in Go and takes very few resources, so 'you can even run it on a Raspberry Pi'. It also says 'Installation is as easy as downloading a binary and a few supporting files, no other dependencies required.'

transparency.note: The README names Musing Studio LLC as the copyright holder. It points to Write.as, 'a hosted service from the team behind WriteFreely', and says paying for it helps 'directly fund our free software work', which tells a reader both who builds it and how it is paid for.

products.name: Funkwhale
products.description: A federated server for music libraries and podcasts, maintained by a non-profit collective, that you can join on an existing pod or run yourself.

openness.note: The LICENSE file in Funkwhale's unified repository is the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3.

accessibility.note: Funkwhale's homepage says 'The easiest way to start using Funkwhale is to register an account on one of the many available pods', while 'Running your own pod requires some system administration skills'. It names two third-party hosts, Weingärtner IT and Cloud68, for people who want a pod run for them.

transparency.note: The homepage says Funkwhale is 'maintained by a non-profit organization called the Funkwhale Collective', credits funding support to the NLnet Foundation and links a donation page. It does not publish financial statements the way Fosstodon's foundation commits to.

products.name: BookWyrm
products.description: A federated social-reading server for tracking, reviewing and discussing books, a fediverse alternative to Goodreads, released under a licence that restricts who may use it.

openness.note: BookWyrm federates over ActivityPub, but its LICENSE is the Anti-Capitalist Software License v1.4, 'released for free use by individuals and organizations that do not operate by capitalist principles'. It allows use only by individuals, non-profits, educational institutions and worker-owned organisations, and bars law enforcement and the military. That is narrower than the open-source licences elsewhere in this list.

accessibility.note: BookWyrm's production install guide opens with a warning: 'This project is still young and isn't, at the moment, very stable, so please proceed with caution when running in production.' It asks for a domain, firewall setup, an outside email service such as Mailgun, and Docker with docker-compose.

longevity.note: BookWyrm's migration guide says an account export includes profile, settings, reading goals, shelves, reading history, reviews, statuses, lists, follows and blocks, and can be imported on another BookWyrm instance. Direct messages, replies, groups and favourites are not included. Moving an account notifies followers 'including followers from non-BookWyrm servers'.

products.name: Hubzilla
products.description: A PHP community server combining social networking, cloud files, blogs, wikis and webpages, built around a portable 'nomadic' identity, with ActivityPub available as an addon.

openness.note: Hubzilla's LICENSE is the permissive MIT licence, granting anyone the right to 'use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell' copies. ActivityPub support is not in the core: it comes from the PubCrawl addon in Hubzilla's separate addons repository.

accessibility.note: Hubzilla's install guide warns that it 'more closely resembles an email server than a web server' and that 'Not every PHP/MySQL hosting provider will be able to support Hubzilla.' It requires PHP 8.2 or later with many extensions, MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL, cron, working outbound mail, and its own domain or subdomain.

longevity.note: Hubzilla's README says 'Migration and live backups of your connections, settings, and everything you publish are built-in, so you never need worry about server failure.' That covers more of an account than Mastodon's follower-only move.

transparency.note: The Hubzilla Association's page says it supports the development, promotion and distribution of Hubzilla and links its articles of association and an imprint. It says members discuss how funds are used in a members-only forum, so the accounts are not public.

products.name: Bluesky
products.description: A mainstream microblogging app built on its company's own open AT Protocol rather than ActivityPub: it supports federated hosting and account portability, but does not natively join the ActivityPub servers in this list.

accessibility.note: Bluesky's App Store listing shows it is free to download, with about 14,000 ratings averaging 3.9 and a #87 chart position in Social Networking. Its version history shows updates through October 2026.

openness.note: Bluesky's FAQ says 'It is a federated network with account portability' built on the AT Protocol. It says that although Bluesky shares the term federation with Mastodon, 'the way it works is very different'. Because it does not use ActivityPub, it does not interoperate directly with the other servers in this roster, unlike Threads' opt-in bridge.

transparency.note: Bluesky's own blog names the investors in its $100M Series B: it was led by Bain Capital Crypto, with Alumni Ventures, Anthos Capital, Bloomberg Beta, Knight Foundation and True Ventures. The post says founder Jay Graber moved to Chief Innovation Officer. The site states Bluesky is a Public Benefit Corporation; the post gives no revenue figures.

longevity.note: The AT Protocol's migration guide describes moving an account's public repository, media and preferences to a new data server and repointing the same identity (DID and handle) at it. 'If the old PDS is inaccessible, a mirror might be available from a public relay, or a local backup might be available.' For a ready-made route the guide points to tools such as goat or the community-built PDS MOOver rather than a button in the app, and it notes some servers lock incoming migrations.
